## Learning the Cluster

A compute cluster is a group of multiple independent computers (nodes) connected to each other so they can work together as one powerful system. Rather than relying on one single computer to do a large analysis consisting of multiple steps, we can send the tasks that make up that analysis as jobs for these independent computers to carry out.

Let's log in to one of the AMNH's clusters, called Mendel.

```
ssh [username]@mendel-master.sdmz.amnh.org
```
You will be prompted to enter your AMNH account password. No text will appear as you type as this is confidential information you don't want your neighbors to see. Once you have completed typing it, hit enter and complete 2-factor authentification.

When you log in you will be greeted with a bunch of information, some clusters do not have this kind of information so readily available but you can research commands to learn the information presented here.

First, you can see what system is runing, the operating system, cluster management tools, and scheduler. A scheduler is what takes all the jobs submitted across users and assigns them start times, compute nodes to be run on, etc. SLURM is a very common one, so is PBS.

Next, you see the queues, these are the names of the different sets of computers on the cluster, you have nodes with different resource availability for running typical jobs (compute nodes) vs more demanding jobs (bigmem) or jobs that require special architecutres (gpu).

If you scroll up you’ll see a list of the programs that are already installed on the cluster. You can also find these anytime with 

```
module avail 
```

**How do you load an application you want to use? **

Type **samtools** into the terminal. You should get an error. Now, load the application (look at the list of available applications) and type it again, **paste the first two lines of output here**.

## Package managers: Conda

Conda is a software manager that lets you create isolated environments so each project has its own versions of tools and dependencies. This avoids version conflicts between tools, makes software installation easily reproducible, keeps your base system clean, and lets each project have its own “sandbox” of programs

A conda environment is like a separate folder that contains its own Python version (if needed), its own installed software, and its own paths and dependencies. If two tools need different versions of the same library, you just put them in different environments.

You activate an environment when you want to use the software inside it, and deactivate it when you're done.

Installing conda. Follow the instructions to install conda. [https://www.anaconda.com/docs/getting-started/miniconda/install\#linux-terminal-installer](https://www.anaconda.com/docs/getting-started/miniconda/install#linux-terminal-installer)

**Warning** A lot of software will default install to your HOME directory ~/$user which on mendel is very space limited (5GB of space). So we have to do an extra step of directing software to our NAS folder. This is especially important for the conda install because we will be building lots of packages which will take up space.

So to avoid the problem listed in the warning, let's get the path of our NAS folders where we want the conda install to go.

```
cd ~/mendel-nas1
pwd #COPY THE OUTPUT
```
Now we can install
```
wget https://repo.anaconda.com/miniconda/Miniconda3-latest-Linux-x86_64.sh
bash Miniconda3-latest-Linux-x86_64.sh
```
**It will ask if you want to install in default file path or another path. You will put in the results of pwd above + /miniconda3 !**

After that, click Yes as initialization option. It notes that we need to exit and relogin for the changes to take place. Let's do that.
```
exit
ssh [username]@mendel-master.sdmz.amnh.org
```
Now you should see ```(base)``` in front of your system details, before the command prompt ($).


Let’s make an environment for today’s lab that will hold all the packages we will need. We will specify the version of python we want and the name of our environment. Then,when we activate it and install the packages, they will be readily available for use.

Conda has different download channels with different kinds of packages. Google “conda install numpy” (a popular python package) and you will see it is in the conda-forge channel. Biology packages usually are in the bioconda package. We will tell the install command to look in this channel for those packages.

```
# Create a conda environment named "genome-assembly"
conda create -n genome-assembly python=3.10

# Activate the environment
conda activate genome-assembly

# Install common genome assembly tools (examples)
conda install -c bioconda seqtk assembly-stats bioawk

# Check installed tools
conda list

#for when you are finished (not now)
#conda deactivate 
```

**Where do your packages live? (What is the path?)**

Here are some important conda commands to know: [https://docs.conda.io/projects/conda/en/4.6.0/\_downloads/52a95608c49671267e40c689e0bc00ca/conda-cheatsheet.pdf](https://docs.conda.io/projects/conda/en/4.6.0/_downloads/52a95608c49671267e40c689e0bc00ca/conda-cheatsheet.pdf)

## Navigating NCBI \- finding sequence read data

We will be using sequence data that has been published on NCBI (National Center for Biotechnology Information). When you publish a paper, the genomic data used in that paper must be published as well, typically to NCBI. Typically the data is published in its rawest form in the **SRA, the Sequence Read Archive.** Each project gets an NCBI BioProject ID that keeps all the genomic data tied to that research. [https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/)

## Downloading sequence data from NCBI

We can use a special program called sra-toolkit to extract these sequences directly to the cluster. This program comes pre-compiled for us in a nice tarball (a form of file compression). We can find the link to download it on their github: [https://github.com/ncbi/sra-tools/wiki/01.-Downloading-SRA-Toolkit](https://github.com/ncbi/sra-tools/wiki/01.-Downloading-SRA-Toolkit)

We want the AlmaLinux version , we can see at the top of mendel that we are running a Linux distribution.  
![][image4]

Copy the link to the distribution with a Right-Click, Copy Link Address. Now in the cluster we are going to type 

```
wget [link]
```

wget is world wide web get and downloads things from the internet. We can typically do simple/quick commands like this from the head node.

Now ls in the directory and you should see a file named sratoolkit.current-alma\_linux64[.tar.gz](http://.tar.gz)

We are going to untar this file:

```
tar -xzvf sratoolkit.[NAME].tar.gz
```

\-x extract  
\-z gzipped (.gz extension)  
\-v verbose output  
\-f file

This should unpack into a directory. We will add the executable to our PATH so we can run this. The PATH variable is a list of directories your shell searches for programs. This is why we amend the path to sra toolkit to the beginning of the path variable, rather than overwriting it.

```
export PATH=$PWD/sratoolkit.[VERSION]-alma_linux64/bin:$PATH
```

The export command adds this to your PATH for your current session/shell, so you would need to do this each time you log-in to the head node or include it in a job script so it adds it to the PATH in those instances.

Now when you type a command that is in the toolkit

```
prefetch
```

It will run that program.

Read the following: [https://github.com/ncbi/sra-tools/wiki/08.-prefetch-and-fasterq-dump](https://github.com/ncbi/sra-tools/wiki/08.-prefetch-and-fasterq-dump)

**What two commands will you run to download the long read sequences?** We will run these now, but they will take a while so we need to create a screen. A screen is a way to have multiple windows available on the head node and they continue to run the commands when closed or you log out. Let's create a screen named download

```
screen -S download
```

Now type your commands and hit enter. You may notice that you can't scroll like in the normal terminal window, rather you press Ctrl+A then [ (or Esc) to enter copy mode. Then, use your arrow keys, Page Up, or Page Down to move through the text. Press Esc again to be able to type normally. To exit the screen (or detach), type Ctrl + A, then press D. You can reattach to it later by typing ```screen -r download```

**WARNING** In the future, we do not want to run any commands on the head node. Starting in the next lab, you will learn how to submit jobs to the nodes to run these tasks.
**Why should you not run things on the head node?**

Check back in your screen a few times until your long read download is complete.

## Compiling programs from GitHub

Visit the GitHub site for hifiasm, a program we will use to assemble a long-read whole genome [https://github.com/chhylp123/hifiasm](https://github.com/chhylp123/hifiasm)

Here, you can see all the materials contained in a single repository for creating hifiasm and running examples. At the bottom, there is a ReadMe file for the program, all programs, whether on github or elsewhere, typically have ReadMe files which include helpful information about program usage.

**Git** is a version control system.  
 It lets you:

* track changes to files (like code or scripts)  
* see who changed what and when  
* go back to earlier versions  
* collaborate without overwriting each other’s work.

Think of it as a **time-machine \+ backup \+ collaboration tool** for projects.

`git clone` makes a **full local copy** of a remote Git repository (e.g., from GitHub).  
 It downloads:

* all files in the project,  
* the entire history of changes,  
* all branches and tags.

```
# Install hifiasm 
git clone https://github.com/chhylp123/hifiasm
```

Let’s list the files in the folder hifiasm 

```
ls hifiasm
```

We can see a bunch of C++ code files (.cpp) and their related headers (.h). We also see something called Makefile. Let’s run the following

```
cd hifiasm && make
```
`make` is a tool that **automates running commands** needed to build or compile software.  
 It looks at a file called a **Makefile**, which lists:

* what needs to be built  
* which files depend on which  
* which commands to run

When you run make it will print g++ commands, this program is used to **compile** the code, converting the documents of code into a program that can be executed (i.e., an **executable**)

You may see many warning messages or notes, typically, these can be disregarded if the test case of your program runs smoothly. ERRORs are the key to look out for as this means the make command failed. 

Now, ls the directory again, we already changed into this directory above (cd) so now we can just ls
 
```
ls
```

You should see executable file is now created in bright green: hifiasm

Now that our program is built we can run the executable in the following way, let’s check out the docs by using \-h (help): 

```
./hifiasm -h  
```

Why do we need `./` before an executable? When you type a command, your shell only looks for programs in the directories listed in your PATH (like `/usr/bin`, `/usr/local/bin`, etc.).

The current directory (`.`) is *not* in your PATH 

So if a program (like `hifiasm`) is sitting in the current folder, your shell won’t find it automatically. Anywhere you want to run this program you will need to specify the full path to the executable:


```
/home/ddebaun/mendel-nas1/Comparative_Genomics_Course/hifiasm/hifiasm -h 
```

Or add it to the directory of your PATH. The export command does this for your current session, so you would need to do this each time or include it in a job script, which we will learn how to construct in the next lab.

Now when you run hifiasm anywhere, it will look in all PATH locations for the executable and execute then.

```
export PATH=/home/ddebaun/mendel-nas1/Comparative_Genomics_Course/hifiasm:$PATH
hifiasm -h 
```
